title: Nickel Mines (2006)
hookLine: an Amish community forgave and embraced the family of the gunman who killed their children

cards: Nickel Mines is a small village in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, in Amish farm country. One morning a man walked into its one-room Amish schoolhouse and shot the girls there.
Some of them died, and so did he, by his own hand. There's no need to say more about that morning. What made people far away stop and look came after.

Soon after, Amish neighbors went to the gunman's family, to say they forgave him, and to comfort his widow and children, who were grieving too. When he was buried, Amish mourners came and stood with that family.

teach.b: Reporters asked how anyone could forgive so fast. The answer pointed back to something old.
The Lord's Prayer runs through Amish worship and home life, and in the King James words it says, "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
Right after the prayer, Jesus adds: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."
Researchers who wrote a book about Nickel Mines, Amish Grace, heard Amish people describe forgiveness as decided long before the day it was needed, prayed into them over years of ordinary mornings.
They didn't have to find it in the worst week of their lives. It had already been chosen, and when the day came, it chose them. It didn't mean the parents stopped grieving.

Forgiving isn't forgetting, and it isn't saying the harm was small; the grief stayed, and had to be walked through. Nor was the matter simple for everyone else. Christians differ on how forgiveness works.
Some point to Jesus in Luke's Gospel, "if he repent, forgive him," and hear forgiveness as waiting on repentance.
Others point to Jesus on the cross: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." There, nobody had asked. Both readings are held in good faith.
At Nickel Mines, the man could never ask. The forgiveness went to his family anyway: a visit, a hand, a presence at the grave.

how: Amish Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home and speak of forgiveness as a choice made ahead of time; after the Nickel Mines shooting, Amish neighbors visited and comforted the gunman's family.

games.q: you're an Amish neighbor. the man who did this is dead, and his widow and children are in a house nearby. what do you do?
o: stay away; it isn't your place.
go to them, to forgive and to comfort.
wait until the anger has passed.
games.why: neighbors went to the family soon after, to say they forgave and to comfort them. they spoke of forgiveness as a choice made long before that day.

practice: Go gently with this one. Think of a family on the other side of some harm, the relatives of someone who hurt others, far away in the news or close to home: a mother, a brother, a child carrying a name they didn't choose.
If you pray, hold them before God; if you don't, simply wish them peace, and if this touches a wound of your own, just rest and breathe.
If it's too heavy, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
